issues.legal_issue: Failure to specify the place of sale in the published notice invalidates a public auction conducted to recover a debt through sale of property.
material_facts: The debtor’s estate was brought to sale by public auction to recover an alleged debt.
The sale publication did not specify the place of sale.
The High Court considered the prescribed form sufficient even though it did not require the place of sale to be stated.
issues.conclusion: The place of sale had to be specified in the published notice; its omission rendered the sale invalid, and the order setting aside the sale was properly restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 36 of the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894, publication of the date and place of sale is mandatory. The word “shall” is construed in light of the provision’s purpose and context. Public notice enables intending bidders to participate, promotes the highest competitive price, and helps ensure fairness and prevent arbitrary or suspicious dealings. The prescribed forms are procedural and cannot override the statute. No earlier cases are cited for this holding.

predicates.revenue_recovery_auction: The proceeding involved a public auction of a debtor’s property to recover a debt through a revenue recovery process.
predicates.sale_notice_omitted_place: The published notice of sale did not state where the sale would take place.
predicates.governing_notice_required_place: The governing sale procedure required the published notice to state the place of sale.

issues.definition: When a revenue recovery auction has a notice that omits the place of sale despite the governing procedure requiring that information, the sale is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser’s failure to pay the balance of the auction price within the required period, absent a court or tribunal order preventing payment, makes confirmation of the sale illegal.
material_facts: The purchaser deposited 15 percent of the sale price at the auction.
The balance was not deposited within 30 days after the auction; it was deposited after the sale had been confirmed and more than a year after the auction.
No court or tribunal order preventing payment within the period was identified.
The purchaser argued that the delay followed protracted correspondence and that the authority’s acceptance of the late payment made confirmation lawful.
issues.conclusion: The balance had to be paid within 30 days unless a court or tribunal order prevented payment. The failure to do so made the deposit liable to forfeiture and confirmation of the sale illegal; the sale was vitiated and was rightly set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 36 of the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1894 requires the balance of the sale consideration to be remitted within 30 days of the auction. The purchaser is obliged to pay within that period unless prevented by an order of a court or tribunal; non-compliance makes the earnest deposit liable to forfeiture, and confirmation without compliance is illegal. No earlier cases are cited for this holding.
